newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Asia bonds find bids in Asia and elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Asia bonds find bids in Asia and elsewhere.

text.p: The percentage of Asian debt paper that stays in the region may be waning as investors in the rest of the world get to know it better.

"Asian issues tend to be well bid out here. But for the issuer that has decided to target either the European or U.S. markets, those bonds tend to stay in those places," said Steve Roberts, managing director at Salomon Brothers in Hong Kong.
Asian bank borrowers have traditionally opted for syndicated floating rate certificate of deposit issues that are marketed locally, or floating rate notes that are syndicated like loans.
Even issues of Asian banks and corporations that are launched Eurobond-style typically end up with Asian lenders.
While this is still the case, bankers in Hong Kong say the market is changing slowly but surely as Asian investors increasingly take their stories to the U.S. and Europe.
YANKEES ARE A HIT

For the most well-known borrowers with the best ratings, such as sovereigns, quasi-sovereigns and major corporations, the favorite venue outside Asia has been the United States because of its large and sophisticated institutional investor base eager to take on longer-dated, higher-yielding paper.

"If you look at some of the frequent borrowers, the investor diversification (of tapping the U.S. market) is particularly compelling," Mark Schneider, vice president at J.P. Morgan Securities in New York, told Reuters.
In early October J.P. Morgan brought a group of mostly U.S. investors to Asia to hear what regional borrowers had to say.
Potential issuers ranging from China's Ministry of Finance to South Korea's quasi-sovereign banks to India's energy companies attended the meeting.
"The U.S. tends to be most cost effective for a borrower with long maturities beyond 10 years," said Salomon's Roberts.

The three-tranche US$1.9 billion global bond recently placed for Malaysian state oil company Petronas by lead managers Salomon Brothers and CS First Boston illustrates where the demand for Asian bonds of different maturities can be found.
Almost all of the US$500 million 30-year tranche placed in the United States, as did about 65 percent of the US$800 million 10-year issue. The rest of the 10-year went to Europe and Asia.
Roberts said 80 percent of the US$600 million five-year bond placed in Europe while 15 percent went to Asian accounts.
Petronas, which already has access to the U.S. market and benefits from name recognition in Asia, actively targetted European investors for this latest issue, Roberts said.
Bankers here said interest in Asian debt is growing in Europe, albeit slowly.
CONQUERING EUROPE

"From our experience, there has been a marked increase in interest and buying out of Europe for the global bonds we have done," said Steve Taran, vice president and senior research director at Lehman Brothers.
At European roadshows for Asian issues, "you do not get people clamouring for a spot at the luncheon table, but you do get a very good response from investors," said Taran.
Just as European political leaders are starting to pay more attention to Asia, so are European investors taking a closer look at the region, Taran said.

He said another factor that could drive demand in future is the trend in many European countries for people to rely more on private, rather than public, savings to fund their retirements. That means there is a growing pool of institutional investors.
Lead manager Merrill Lynch said last month that its five-year Eurobond for Philippines Commercial International Bank attracted first-time European, as well as U.S. investors.

"We were able to find crossover European investors and select U.S. investors who were buying Philippine paper for first time, as well as the more traditional Asian investors who bought on an asset-swapped basis," Tom Seaman, managing director at Merrill Lynch, said after the issue closed.
HOMEWARD BOUND
Critics say most of the Asian bonds that sell in Europe make their way back to Asia, largely through the asset swappers that convert the fixed rate paper to floating rate.
"Of the fixed-rate Eurobonds, probably about 70 percent ends up in Asia including Japan and 30 percent in Europe," estimated Bob Janjuah, global head of credit research at SBC Warburg.
But much depends on the issuer, Janjuah added.
"A lot of the Korean paper goes to Europe, but BB credits, like the Indonesian and Philippines corporates, tend to stay in Asia," he said.
Paul Smith, executive director of capital markets at Union Bank of Switzerland in Hong Kong, said Asians remain the biggest buyers of Asian paper.

"We've always taken the view that outside the story issues in the U.S. where they are specifically targetted to the pension funds, the real support for Asian names and where the credits are far better understood is here in Asia," he said.
"It is interesting that the Asian investor market is beginning to be recognised as something of depth with very much sustainability," he added.
A US$600 million floating rate note issue for Indonesia's APP Global Finance launched in September by UBS was snapped up in Asia, mostly by accounts in Taiwan and Korea.
But the market for fixed rate paper is thinner in Asia than in the U.S. and Europe because pension funds and insurance companies are just starting to establish themselves here.
SBC's Janjuah estimated that half of Asia's buyers of fixed rate paper are institutions and half are professional traders.
"In Asia, a lot (of fixed rate paper) goes into the street, a lot of it is for banks' own account trading and a lot is going to asset swappers," he said.
FLOWBACK ARGUMENT FLAWED
While acknowledging that a significant portion of Asian debt flows back to Asia, some bankers said that the amount of paper that flows back is dwindling -- or that flowback doesn't matter.

"I think very little of it is coming back to Asia. We are seeing strong demand in Europe...and we are confident that pattern is going to continue," said Ian Adams, head of debt security new issues at Banque Nationale de Paris in Hong Kong.
Salomon's Roberts said the concept of flowback doesn't mean much because funds now flow easily through much of the world.

"The lines that were previously drawn between paper that traded in the U.S., Europe and Asia have become much greyer, so it is becoming almost meaningless as to whether it is an Asian bond, a Eurobond, a Yankee bond or whatever," he said.

For bank lenders, the lines are even fuzzier. A bank's Singapore branch will make a more aggressive bid for Asian paper than its Frankfurt head office simply because it has a mandate from the head office to build up regional assets, Roberts said.
